context: In IP Australia Economic Research Paper 01 (2014), *Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency*, the opening publication details identify the report, its author and acknowledgments, and provide its suggested citation and copyright information.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, the Executive Summary analyses IP Australia’s patent application inventory and pendency, comparing inventory measures with the UK Intellectual Property Office and US Patent and Trademark Office. It describes inventory trends from 2000 to early 2013, examiner staffing, and changes in exit pendency for applications filed in Australia.

In the 2014 *Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency*, the Executive Summary discusses examination-request timing and application acceptance rates in IP Australia’s deferred examination system, then summarises changes in patent pendency and inventories through 2009 and recommends prioritising older applications.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, the Introduction describes the analysis of IP Australia’s standard-patent backlog using publicly available data from January 1995 to May 2013. It explains that the report applies a backlog framework to estimate application inventories and compare them across countries.

In the 2014 report *Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency*, the Methodology section explains a four-waypoint framework for measuring standard patent application stocks at IP Australia and comparing inventories across countries. The waypoints are Receipt, Ripe, Decision and Disposal, from an application’s receipt through its grant or early termination.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, the “Defining Stocks” section explains how IP Australia divides standard patent applications into three stages of the inventory, from receipt to final disposal, and distinguishes applications awaiting action by the office from those awaiting action by applicants.

In the “Defining Stocks” section of IP Australia’s 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, this passage recommends recording inbound and outbound correspondence to distinguish applications awaiting action by the office from those awaiting action by applicants. It notes that existing administrative data do not show when applications are sent between them.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, the Pendency section defines two ways to measure patent application pendency: time to disposal for applications ending in the same month (exit pendency) and for applications filed in the same month (entry pendency). The report estimates both, but not the unobservable expected pendency discussed in the cited joint report.

In the 2014 report *Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency*, this section explains IP Australia’s patent application process and its deferred examination system, including examination requests, opposition and grant. The preceding text distinguishes observable pendency measures from expected pendency, which the report does not produce.

In the 2014 report *Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency*, the “Process in numbers” section explains Figure 4, which tracks the progress of IP Australia’s 2008 patent application filing cohort through May 2013; the percentages are shares of all applications filed that year.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, this figure describes the progress of IP Australia’s 2008 patent application cohort through the administrative process, including its grant, lapse or other non-grant, pending, and accepted-but-waiting outcomes by May 2013.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, Section 3, “Patent Application Inventories,” describes IP Australia’s patent application inventory from 2000 to 2013 and compares total inventory with the US and UK. It explains the growth and decline in total and unexamined applications and identifies stock 1 as applications not yet ready for examination.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, Section 3, “Patent Application Inventories,” this passage explains changes in IP Australia’s patent application stocks from 2007 to 2013, including the effects of examination requests and the Raising the Bar reforms, and compares stock distributions in Australia, the US and UK.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, section 3, this passage describes IP Australia’s patent application inventory from 2000 to 2012. It compares the proportions in stocks 1, 2 and 3, noting stock 1’s dominance, stock 2’s share in relation to examiner stock-out concerns, and a peak that coincided with fewer examiners.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, section 4 examines how IP Australia’s examiner numbers and patent application filings relate to inventory levels. It discusses Figure 11 and trends in applications and stock per examiner, including changes from 2000 to 2012.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, section 4 compares patent application stocks per examiner at IP Australia, the UK-IPO and USPTO. It discusses annual figures and notes that Australia’s deferred examination model allows applications to remain pending longer before examination.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, this section examines how pending patent application stocks relate to pendency at the USPTO and UK-IPO, and explains that IP Australia measures pendency as the time for an application to leave its inventory.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, the Exit Pendency section explains how exit pendency measures the time granted patent applications spend in IP Australia’s system. It describes changes in average and median exit pendency, and its distribution, for applications granted from 2000 to 2013.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, in the “Exit Pendency” section, this passage describes changes in Australian patent application exit pendency from 2000 to 2013 and compares median pendency trends with the USPTO and UK-IPO, noting differences in examination-request timing.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, the “Entry Pendency” section examines how long IP Australia applications take to reach grant, by filing cohort. It discusses trends among applications filed from 1995 onward, including a rise around June 2002 and possible links to examiner numbers.

In the 2014 *Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency*, the Entry Pendency section compares patent application entry pendency in Australia, the US and the UK. It reports grant times for applications filed in 2008 and points to similar international trends in entry and exit pendency.

In the 2014 *Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency*, the “Effects of Direction” section explains how IP Australia’s examination directions affect patent pendency and stock 1, and motivates comparing directed with voluntary examination requests, including for the 2008 application cohort.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, the “Directed vs. Voluntary Examination Requests” section compares when applicants requested patent examination and the resulting acceptance rates for applications filed from 1995 to 2008. It explains the contrast between requests made after IP Australia directed applicants to seek examination and requests made voluntarily.

In the 2014 report *Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency*, the “Directed vs. Voluntary Examination Requests” section compares acceptance rates for Australian patent applications directed to examination and those requested voluntarily. It describes changes from 2000 to 2008 and notes that grants on voluntary requests remained relatively stable.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, section 7, “Stockpiles by International Patent Classification,” this passage explains how the report analyses patent backlogs by each application’s first IPC code and how IPC classes relate to IP Australia’s examination groups.

In the 2014 *Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency*, in the section on examination groups, the table maps main International Patent Classification (IPC) sections A–G to IP Australia’s examination groups. An “X” marks the groups to which applications in each IPC section are allocated.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, this table in the section on stockpiles by International Patent Classification maps the eight main technology classes to exam groups for their initial allocation in June 2013. The preceding text explains that the report examines patent application inventories by technology class and recommends collecting exam-group inventory data for backlog and workforce planning.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, this section examines IP Australia’s patent application inventory in IPC class A, Human Necessities. It describes changes in the three inventory stocks from 2000 to 2012, including their shares and levels, and notes that this class is the largest share of total inventory.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, this section examines patent application inventories by International Patent Classification, focusing on class B (Performing Operations; Transporting). It describes changes in the class B stocks from 2005 onward, including how increases in Stock 1 relate to later increases in Stocks 2 and 3.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, this section examines patent application inventories in IPC classification C (Chemistry). It describes changes in stocks 1 and 2 and overall inventory levels from 2000 onward, including possible explanations for the stock 2 pattern.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, the IPC class D section examines Australian patent application inventories for Textiles and Paper. It describes monthly stock levels from 2000 to 2011, including changes in stocks 1, 2 and 3 and D’s share of the total inventory.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, this passage examines patent application inventories in IPC section E (Fixed Construction). It describes growth from 2000 to 2012, the contribution of stock 1, and the lack of corresponding examination requests.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, the section on IPC Section F covers patent application inventory in mechanical engineering, lighting, heating, weapons and blasting. It describes inventory trends from 2000 to 2013, including a 2012–13 rise in stock 1 and its relation to new filings and examination requests.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, the IPC section G—Physics discussion examines patent application inventory trends from 2000 onward. It describes changes in overall inventory and stocks 1, 2 and 3, and G’s share of total inventory.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, the section on IPC class H (Electricity) describes changes in patent application inventory and stock levels from 2000 to 2012, including a sharp rise in Stock 1 in 2012.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, the “Pendency by Technology” section compares patent application processing times across the eight main international patent classification (IPC) sections. It explains that Figure 30 shows average entry-pendency differences from the overall mean, including faster processing for 2008 applications classified in Section H (Electricity).

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, the conclusion summarizes changes in IP Australia’s patent application inventory and examination pendency from 2000 to 2013, and describes factors and workflow practices associated with those changes.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, the Recommendations section proposes data and workflow improvements for managing IP Australia’s patent examination inventories and pendency. It recommends tracking inside and outside inventories, application complexity, fast-tracked applications, exam-group allocations in PAMS, and examiner capacity.

In the recommendations of IP Australia’s 2014 *Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency*, the passage recommends a formal process for prioritizing patent applications sent to examination groups, potentially matching cases to examiners by technology, specialisation or inventory rather than releasing them in bulk.

In the 2014 *Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency*, Appendix 1’s “Priority Filing” section explains how provisional patent applications establish a priority date, how that date relates to assessing novelty and inventive step against prior art, and how multiple provisional applications may be combined into a complete application.

In the 2014 *Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency*, Appendix 1’s section on International PCT Filing explains that applicants can file a complete patent application under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, designating its member jurisdictions, including Australia, and securing an international priority date.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, Appendix 1’s “IP Australia Complete Filing” section explains complete patent applications in Australia: the 12-month filing period, required contents, priority claims based on provisional applications, and divisional applications treated as separate applications for the report.

In the 2014 *Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency*, Appendix 1’s “Request for Examination” section explains the deadlines for requesting examination of a complete Australian patent application: five years from completion, or six months after IP Australia directs the applicant to request examination. Missing the applicable deadline causes the application to lapse.

In the 2014 *Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency*, Appendix 1’s “Search” section describes IP Australia’s patent application process. It explains that applications entering the national phase without a prior-art search or international examination receive an extensive search by a team of three examiners, while abbreviated examinations do not include a search.

In the 2014 *Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency*, Appendix 1 describes the Australian patent examination process. This passage explains how examination assesses patentability against the Patents Act and prior art, and how an examiner’s first report and the applicant’s response address objections.

In the 2014 *Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency*, Appendix 1’s account of the Australian patent prosecution process explains further examination and reports. It describes reports following applicant responses, the 21-month deadline after a first report, and senior-examiner review in a third examination round.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, in the appendix section on results of IP Australia’s patent prosecution process, this passage describes the three final outcomes for a patent application and the publication and opposition period that follows.

In the 2014 Report on patent backlogs, inventories and pendency, the Appendix 1 section “Opposition and Hearing” describes how patent applications may be granted, amended or refused after public opposition and hearings. It also notes that the 2013 Patent Act changes reduced the relevant period to 12 months, which is excluded from the historical inventory analysis.

The opening pages of *The market for design: insights from interviews with Australian firms* (2014), IP Australia Economic Research Paper 03, give the report title, authors and suggested citation. The report examines the market for design through interviews with Australian firms.

In the acknowledgments of *The market for design: insights from interviews with Australian firms* (2014), the authors thank IP Australia for supporting the research, the study participants for sharing their experiences, and Benjamin Mitra-Kahn for guidance.

In the 2014 report *The market for design: insights from interviews with Australian firms*, the Copyright section states that the publication is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0, with exceptions for specified Commonwealth and IP Australia material and possible third-party permissions.

The 2014 IP Australia Economic Research Paper *The market for design* executive summary describes interviews about how Australia’s design market operates. It explains the limited role of design rights and how buyers and sellers use reputation signals—the 5 R’s and 4 C’s—to manage transactions and value.

In *The Market for Design* (2014), Section 1.1, “Background and Motivation,” this passage discusses design’s growing importance and employment in Australia, and compares Australian design application levels and growth with patents, including Figure 1’s 2008–13 applications.

In the 2014 report *The Market for Design: Insights from Interviews with Australian Firms*, the Introduction’s Background and Motivation section considers why Australian design registrations have low visibility and growth, and whether design rights are useful only in certain contexts or alongside other IP rights and firms’ management practices. The passage introduces the project’s investigation of design protection and how firms use design.

In *The market for design* (2014), Section 1.2, “Scope,” describes an interview study of Australian firms on how design relates to marketing, strategy, intellectual property protection and firm performance. It examines buyers’ and sellers’ perspectives and the ways they use reputation signals to address uncertainty in design transactions.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the prior-research section on design as a process, this passage reviews how management, economics, and design research describe designers’ work and design thinking. It also notes that the study is a precursor to a future survey.

In The market for design (2014), the “Design as an artifact” section reviews research on design as a marketable product: how firms use intellectual property and alternatives such as non-imitability to protect designs, signal distinctiveness, negotiate and compete, including through imitation.

In the 2014 report *The market for design: insights from interviews with Australian firms*, the “Design as an artifact” section reviews research on how managing and revealing design-related intellectual property can enable collaboration and innovation while increasing exposure to imitation and loss of specialised knowledge.

In *The Market for Design: Insights from Interviews with Australian Firms* (2014), in the prior research discussion of design as a capability, this passage reviews literature on how firms’ design capabilities help them adapt to industry transitions, dominant designs and technological discontinuities.

In *The market for design: insights from interviews with Australian firms* (2014), the “Design as a capability” section reviews research on design’s effects on economic performance and firms, noting limited Australian firm-level research and asking how firms capture value from building and selling design capabilities.

In *The market for design* (2014), the “Design as a capability” section discusses how leading design firms convey information about their organisational settings and use signals to overcome market frictions and co-create and capture value from design. It connects this issue to whether advanced economies can specialise in design while manufacturing takes place in lower-cost countries.

In the methodology section of *The Market for Design* (2014), this passage describes semi-structured interviews with senior executives at Australian firms, including how interviewees and buyer-seller pairs were selected and which market, appropriability and firm-level topics the interviews addressed.

In *The market for design* (2014), section 2, “Methodology,” this passage lists the organizations and interviewees in the Australian design-market interview set and explains that the report’s findings draw on seven formal interviews, supplemented where possible by informal interviews and public information.

In *The market for design: insights from interviews with Australian firms* (2014), Section 3, “Key Findings,” this passage introduces findings from interviews with buyers and sellers about design-led differentiation and intellectual property rights. It notes that firms see formal IP protection as playing a limited role in their market strategies.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the section “Imitation: designs are not easily protected,” this case study describes how Australian skincare company Aesop’s use of readily available packaging and design components limits formal IP protection and leaves its brand open to imitation in Australia and internationally.

In the Aesop case study in *The Market for Design* (2014), part of the section on formal IP protection, the passage describes the Australian cosmetics and personal-care firm’s design-led brand and store approach, and the limited role of formal IP protection amid imitation in Australia and internationally.

In *The market for design* (2014), the Aesop case study in the findings on formal IP protection describes Aesop’s reuse of a former partner’s ladder design for its Chelsea store and its view that respecting a design partner’s work is a matter of both agreement and personal trust.

In the 2014 report *The market for design*, this example in the section on Broached Commissions discusses how the Australian furniture design company respects a private client’s request to keep a commissioned table design exclusive, and the risk of alienating the client by making a similar design for others.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the findings section on formal IP protection, Henry Wilson explains why registering designs and patents is not the best use of his time, preferring to focus on producing designs first and affordably.

In the 2014 report *The Market for Design*, in the section on Henry Wilson under the theme that formal IP protection plays a limited role, this passage describes his view that pursuing patents and design registration is not worth the time because Australian protections seem ineffective; he instead protects his name and brand with a trademark.

In *The market for design* (2014), the section on how intellectual property rights can impede creative processes describes Molonglo Group director Nectar Efkarpidis’s perspective, in the context of the NewActon development and its collaborative work across design and other creative fields.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the case study on Molonglo Group under the theme that formal IP protection plays a limited role, the passage describes the Canberra company’s design-led activities and its view that registered design rights are less central than people working together and encouraging others to adopt its design approach.

In the 2014 report *The market for design*, in the section on Molonglo Group under findings about IP protection, this passage describes the company’s view that design’s value lies in creating places people adopt and shape, rather than in design rights.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the section on market participants viewing design as a capability, this passage explains why Australian design-market interviewees give limited attention to design rights: they emphasise organisational and collaborative capabilities, rather than design as a protectable artifact.

In *The market for design: insights from interviews with Australian firms* (2014), in the findings section on design as a capability, this passage cites Molonglo Group’s view that design expertise is embedded in people, their shared working practices and collaboration with clients, rather than in an individual designer. The note gives the source for Molonglo Group’s history.

In *The market for design: insights from interviews with Australian firms* (2014), under Theme 2, “The impact of weak intellectual property on the market for design,” this passage explains how limited design-rights protection complicates cooperative trade in design ideas between firms, before products or services are made or delivered.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the findings on how weak formal IP protection affects the market for design, this passage describes sellers’ difficulty capturing value when buyers may take their design ideas and execute them without buying the design service.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the section on how weak intellectual property protections make it difficult for design sellers to capture value, this case describes Right Angle Studio’s experience with a hotel developer who used its rooftop-cinema ideas without proceeding with the proposed joint venture.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the “Crowd Productions” example under Theme 2 on weak intellectual property and value capture, the passage describes a London- and Melbourne-based design practice and its effort to explain design’s cost and value to clients. It notes that the bespoke nature of commissions can make it difficult for design sellers to capture value from buyers.

In *The market for design* (2014), under the discussion of how weak intellectual property protection affects the market for design, this passage explains how the unique, one-off nature of a commissioned design can make it difficult for sellers to build a scalable business and price the work to cover re-engineering costs.

In *The market for design* (2014), under Theme 2 on weak intellectual property protections, this DCM interview describes how a government design contest exposed the Melbourne architecture firm’s work to use by the winning entrant without payment.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the section on buyers capturing value from design sellers, this passage introduces interviewees’ concerns about adverse selection and moral hazard in the market for design.

In *The market for design* (2014), this passage in the section on buyers capturing value from design sellers explains adverse selection: buyers may lack information about design quality, as illustrated by John Denton’s account of public architecture tenders under Public Private Partnerships.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the section on buyers’ challenges capturing value from design sellers, this passage discusses moral hazard and low initial architectural design fees that may rise through charges for changes to the specification.

In *The market for design* (2014), the findings section examines how buyers capture value from design sellers in Australia. This passage discusses underquoting and incomplete contract specifications in building design, and Molonglo Group’s view that iterative design requires continued collaboration as projects evolve.

In *The Market for Design* (2014), in the section on buyers’ challenges in capturing value from design sellers, a firm describes design as an iterative process requiring collaboration and says it dismissed a practice that would not collaborate in the way it wanted.

In *The market for design* (2014), Theme 3 discusses how sellers of design services address market challenges, including risks from weak IP protection. It describes reputation and other signals as supporting trade in high-design services, and groups sellers’ signals into five categories: rigour, rhetoric, rating, roster and referral.

In *The market for design* (2014), this passage is in the section on how buyers assess design sellers and concerns “rigour” as a signal of effort and quality in Australian design services. It describes Broached Commissions’ gallery exhibitions and Crowd Productions’ use of strategic design to demonstrate rigour and encourage early involvement.

In *The Market for Design* (2014), in the section on rigour as a way for design sellers to show commitment to high effort, this passage discusses Crowd Productions’ strategic design process and how experience and partly tacit methods may help distinguish the firm and guard against imitation.

In *The market for design* (2014), the findings section on rigour examines how Crowd Productions signals effort and expertise to corporate buyers in Australia’s market for design, helping clients trust its process and the firm capture value.

In *The Market for Design* (2014), in the section on rigour as a signal of seller effort, this passage describes Crowd Productions’ workshop-based prototyping process and how National Australia Bank adopted it to build design capability. It also explains NAB manager Louise Long’s emphasis on an agency’s adaptability, reputation and methodology when selecting external design suppliers.

In *The market for design: insights from interviews with Australian firms* (2014), under Theme 2’s discussion of how buyers capture value from design sellers, this passage gives a possible explanation for why new entrants may be disadvantaged: time-compression diseconomies.

In the 2014 report *The market for design: insights from interviews with Australian firms*, this case study in the section on buyers’ challenges in capturing value from design describes NAB’s use of design in its branches and workplaces, including a customer-focused branch design initiative begun in 2006 and recognition for its Melbourne headquarters in 2014.

In The market for design (2014), the section on “Rhetoric” examines how Australian design sellers share their expertise and design philosophy to signal quality and engage buyers early, despite risks from weak or absent IP protection. It discusses Crowd Productions’ design narrative and the value of revealing some design knowledge while respecting its proprietary value.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the section on “Rhetoric” as a buyer strategy for assessing design sellers, this passage describes how Australian design firms signal expertise and design philosophy, including through openness, qualifications and respect for intellectual property.

In *The Market for Design* (2014), in the section on rhetoric as a way buyers assess a design seller’s expertise and philosophy, this passage describes how Right Angle Studio’s free content helped demonstrate its ability to engage and curate communities and led to design commissions.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the section on rhetoric as a way buyers assess design sellers, this passage describes how Broached Commissions and Aesop use narrative, communication and design philosophy to demonstrate expertise and connect with communities and markets.

In the 2014 report *The market for design*, in the section on rhetoric as a way buyers assess design sellers, this passage describes Aesop’s use of locally tailored store design and architecture to shape how the firm is perceived when entering markets, illustrated by its launch in Berlin, Germany.

In *The market for design* (2014), under Theme 2’s discussion of buyer strategies for evaluating design sellers, this passage explains how external endorsements such as awards and gallery collections signal design quality and can help Australian designers build professional standing, win work, and commercialise products.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the section on external validation of design sellers’ ability, skill or prestige, this passage describes how competitions and awards helped architect John Denton and Denton Corker Marshall build capabilities, reputation and business, and how awards can signal market-relevant expertise.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the section on “Rating”—external validation of a design seller’s ability, skill or prestige—the passage describes how recognition from trusted critics and experts can help Australian design firms attract clients and build brand prestige. It includes examples from Henry Wilson, Aesop and Broached Commissions.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the section on rating as a way buyers assess design sellers, the passage discusses how imitation may signal a designer’s reputation and affect the prestige of a luxury brand.

In *The market for design* (2014), the section “Roster” examines how design firms use the quality and prestige of their clients to signal capability and work quality, including how early-stage and established designers approach client rosters.

In *The market for design* (2014), the section “Roster—quality and prestige of prior clients” discusses how an architecture firm’s reputation and client roster shape which design projects it pursues, including its decision to focus on selected work rather than chase projects to maintain turnover.

In the 2014 report *The market for design*, this section examines how the quality and prestige of prior clients help Australian design sellers market their work, using examples from architecture and product design. It also discusses commercial models for high-design practices, including mass production, licensing, royalties and joint ventures.

In *The Market for Design* (2014), in the section on referrals under the theme of weak intellectual property protection, this passage explains how recommendations from clients or associates can help Australian design firms build trust with buyers, while not always resolving information gaps. It gives examples involving Broached Commissions and an architect’s work for a Chinese buyer.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the section on referrals as a way for buyers to assess design sellers, this passage explains how a former associate’s recommendation helped John Denton overcome uncertainty about a Chinese buyer, while the buyer’s US$5,000 payment signalled seriousness.

In *The market for design* (2014), Theme 4 examines how buyers in Australia’s market for design use four strategies—contests, co-creation, curation and casting—to reduce uncertainty and overcome challenges when dealing with sellers. It includes Henry Wilson’s point that sellers may not know whether buyers understand the cost of design quality.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the section on buyer strategies in the market for design, this passage explains how contests can reduce the risks of buying design services when buyers cannot assess design quality in advance and intellectual property rights offer little assurance.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the section on contests as a way for buyers to assess design sellers, this passage explains how competitions can reduce information gaps through sellers’ submissions and comparisons. It also describes how contest structures signal buyer commitment and the risks of assigning intellectual property in Australian architecture competitions.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the section on contests as a way for buyers to induce sellers to reveal information, this passage describes Denton Corker Marshall’s view that winning design competitions matters to the firm’s success and that it has developed skills for designing quickly and efficiently to win them.

In *The market for design* (2014), the section on co-creation examines how buyers’ costly involvement in Australian design projects can help address moral hazard between buyers and design sellers. The example is Molonglo Group’s collaboration with designers on Hotel Hotel in Canberra.

In *The Market for Design* (2014), in the section on co-creation under Theme 2, this passage explains how buyers’ time, effort and openness in working with Australian design suppliers signal commitment and help inspire high-design work.

In *The Market for Design* (2014), in the section on co-creation under the theme of weak intellectual property’s impact on the design market, this passage describes how buyers’ participation and design knowledge help them work with Australian design firms. It contrasts collaborative clients with buyers who expect a quick, one-way commission.

In *The Market for Design* (2014), in the section on co-creation as a buyer strategy, the passage describes how buyers contribute knowledge and informed choices to the design process, and how designers may trade off immediate fees for project quality and reputation.

In *The market for design* (2014), this section examines curation as a way buyers signal sophistication and genuine interest in design, influencing sellers’ choices in design transactions. It describes Molonglo Group’s acquisition of a ceramic collection for Hotel Hotel and how its past work and collaborators helped persuade the artist’s family to sell.

In *The market for design: insights from interviews with Australian firms* (2014), the section on curation examines how design businesses use carefully chosen partners, products, clients and exhibition settings to signal their sensibilities and credibility. Examples from Aesop, Molonglo Group and Broached Commissions show how curation can attract customers, build networks and support future business opportunities.

In the 2014 report *The market for design*, this passage in the findings section on curation explains how involvement in the Hotel Hotel development helped Right Angle Studio build networks and reputation, while noting that curation may bring less direct business value to firms whose design work is not a tangible artefact.

In *The Market for Design* (2014), the section on casting examines how Australian design buyers appoint key people to specific roles to reduce information-asymmetry risks, including the risk that sellers act against the buyer’s interests. The passage uses Molonglo Group’s selection process as an example.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the section on casting as a way buyers assess design suppliers, this passage describes selecting and assigning key people to roles, maintaining a roster of external designers, and using endorsements and community ties to signal commitment and trustworthiness.

In *The market for design* (2014), in the section on casting—appointing key personnel to specific roles—the passage describes how Aesop manages relationships with design service providers to signal commitment to creative communities and build lasting alliances as partners’ capabilities and reputations develop.

In *The market for design* (2014), section 4, “Discussion and links to policy,” this passage describes the study’s interview-based method and its findings about the limited role of formal IP protection and how weak IP rights impede Australia’s design market.

In the 2014 report *The market for design: insights from interviews with Australian firms*, section 4, “Discussion and links to policy,” discusses interview findings on Australian design businesses. It explains why design and other IP rights are seen as having limited relevance when design is co-created as a service, and how buyers and sellers use strategies to transact despite weak perceived protection.

In *The market for design: insights from interviews with Australian firms* (2014), the Discussion and links to policy section describes how design buyers and sellers use reputational signals to address transaction challenges where formal IP protection is seen as weak or of limited relevance.

In *The market for design* (2014), section 4.1, “Considerations for the Review of the Designs System,” the passage discusses how Australian design-market participants’ behaviour and views on design rights may inform the 2014 ACIP review, including the system’s duration, grace period, harmonisation and overlap with other IP rights.

In *The Market for Design* (2014), section 4.1 discusses policy considerations for the 2014 Review of Australia’s Designs System. It argues that raising awareness of design rights alone may not increase uptake, and that review policy should consider market segments, interviewees’ 5Rs and 4Cs, and how buyers and sellers co-create design value.

In *The market for design: insights from interviews with Australian firms* (2014), section 4.2, “Broader Implications,” this passage discusses how Australian firms build design capability and reputation, identifying four enablers and indicators relevant to policy: nurturing talent, communicating design processes, gaining recognition, and attracting high-quality clients.

In *The market for design: insights from interviews with Australian firms* (2014), this passage discusses nurturing talent in Australia’s design industry.
